column1: # Test 1's blind reviews. Round 1's local runs: set test1-20261111-1304, graded by Opus (of 16). Round 2's local runs with round 1's Sonnet and Terra runs, regraded: set test1-20261112-1410, graded by Sol through Codex on Sherlock (of 21; Terra, a contestant, didn't grade). Iteration 3 (round3, with Flash-Next redone after the placeholder-check fix, round3-sonnet and round3-terra): set test1-20261113-0923, graded against the F1-F7 checklist by Sol through Codex and by Opus, reconciled (of 21). One line a complete run.

column7: note
All rules right and both apps planned in parallel with mirrored tests; but invents a 52-workday search horizon and steps candidate starts on a grid, and leaves Flask vs stdlib open.

Every rule stated right, standard library, minute-by-minute scan finds the true earliest slot, integer cents rounded once; but lets a rebooked job end after 17:00, where only the extended job may, and adds a search horizon.
Thorough and both apps covered, but the booking search steps in 20-minute increments and stops at 30 days, so it can miss the earliest slot and refuse jobs the problem says to book.
Thorough, but FR-002 requires the two apps to stay in sync, which the problem puts out of scope; adds a 90-day horizon.
Spec right, but the mobile app is three tasks at the end, the search uses a 20-minute grid, and utilization is built before booking.
Calls the workday 8 hours (it is 9), never states the $45 rate in the spec; otherwise covers both apps.
Adds offline sync the problem excludes, plans a CLI, gives the Swift package 6 tasks and makes tests optional.
8-hour workday error; plans an iOS app on CoreData with FastAPI rather than a UI-less Swift package.
No mobile app at all (Python FastAPI in Docker), and rebooks a bumped job at exactly +1 h instead of by the booking rule.
Calls the workday 8 hours (it is 9); plans a FastAPI back end and an iOS app with screens on UIKit, but no Swift tasks at all.
Same as aa714f: stack undecided, no Swift tasks, deletion rules and error handling missing.
Plan leaves language and platform as NEEDS CLARIFICATION, no Swift tasks, and the spec omits the deletion rules and per-cleaner invoice lines.
Most buildable: both local apps, exact earliest-slot candidates without a cutoff, atomic cascades, preserved invoices, and day-split utilization are specified and ordered in the tasks.

Covers both apps and all core rules with a finite search derived from existing jobs, atomic cascades, invoice snapshots, and shared fixtures; utilization attributes overnight work to the job's start day.
Detailed two-app tasks and parity cases make this useful, but its 366-day search cutoff can refuse a later valid slot, and it truncates tap times to whole minutes before billing.

Clear dual-app design, second-precision billing, and conformance cases; the arbitrary 366-day booking bound violates the unbounded earliest-slot rule, and utilization assigns all work to the Arrive date.
Concrete APIs, parity scenarios, and well-sequenced tasks cover both apps, but the invented 60-day booking horizon rejects requests the stated rule would place later.
Broad two-app coverage and sensible task order, but its 15-minute booking scan can miss the actual earliest available start after a variable-length job.
Strong two-app structure and cascade worklist, but utilization is incorrectly capped at 8 and 40 hours and the model permits cancelling in-progress jobs on client deletion.
Detailed mirrored Python and Swift work covers most flows, but it repeatedly calls 8 hours the maximum job length, wrongly refusing valid jobs of up to 9 hours.
Both apps and major workflows are planned, but the research's cents formula uses worked_minutes times 45 divided by 60 instead of times 4500 divided by 60; its 365-day cutoff also breaks booking.

Gets the 9-hour limit and most business rules right, but the mobile tasks cover mainly time and storage rather than the same full rule set, and the desktop is planned as a process rather than a defined local web page.

Provides both app contracts and ordered tasks, but says an exactly 9-hour job is too long, gives a wrong overlap predicate in research, and shows invoice amounts three times the correct charge in its data example.
Covers many features in both languages, but plans one shared data file despite the separate-local-file limit and refuses valid jobs longer than 8 hours.
The Python task list gives useful detail for booking, cascade, billing, and removals, but delivers only a CLI and omits the required Python-served web page and Swift package.
Substantial domain coverage, including the correct 9-hour limit and chained rebooking, but the implementation is a single Python CLI with neither required app form.
Plans a local Python API and most workflows, but omits the Swift package and explicitly imposes an incorrect 8-hour job limit.
Has extensive requirements and a Python API outline, but no Swift package or coherent web-page tasks; deletion tasks refuse future jobs instead of rebooking or cancelling them.
Plans a Python CLI only, rejects valid 8-to-9-hour jobs, and leaves the required desktop web page and Swift package unbuilt.
A single Python CLI replaces both required app forms; it also gives jobs a 2-to-3-hour duration and computes invoices from cleaner count rather than each cleaner's recorded time.
Thin single-project Python plan lacks the Swift package, a specified local web page, and enough implementation detail for safe cascading and error handling.
Leaves language, platform, dependencies, and testing as NEEDS CLARIFICATION, then lists only a generic Python CLI; the required two-app implementation cannot be built from it.

Although the spec and plan name both app forms, the task list switches paths and invents grace-period extension charges, half-day utilization values, and deletion of issued invoices, requiring extensive rework.

Passes F1-F7 and follows every rule: page with a day view and tap buttons, shared conformance scenarios, failed cascades change nothing; 20 gaps recorded (one job in progress per cleaner can refuse an Arrive).
Passes F1-F7 and follows every rule: split jobs booked as complete sequences, atomic cascades, invoices aggregated across parts; tasks less specific than Sonnet run 1 (Sol ranked it first; tied).
Fit: Arrive/Depart are desktop API routes (no button needed, owner 13 Nov). Refuses lengths off the quarter hour (recorded; Sol failed it on these), so some valid requests need rounding.
Fit: Arrive/Depart are desktop API routes (no button needed, owner 13 Nov). Split-job parts fixed at 8:00, so long jobs book later than possible. The only fit local plan.

F6: its invoice test expects $157.50 + $202.50 = $337.50 (the sum is $360.00). Otherwise complete, page with taps; refuses a long job whose first-found cleaners cannot take a later part; a DST test uses a nonexistent time.
F6: a job over 8 hours gets one Arrive/Depart pair for all its days, so its invoice bills the nights or issues after day one. Sol passed it.
F4: back-office taps are coded but no route or page reaches them, so the back office never issues an invoice; a cleaner deletion that cannot rebook cancels the job (Sol: F6).
F4: back-office taps are coded but no route or page reaches them, so the back office never issues an invoice. Sol passed it; its interface lists no tap route.
F4: back-office taps are coded but no route or page reaches them, so the back office never issues an invoice. Sol passed it; its page lists no taps.
F4: its desktop contract puts Arrive/Depart off the web page, so the back office never issues an invoice. Sol passed it.
F4, F6: refuses deleting any cleaner or client who has worked a job; no back-office tap route; one Arrive/Depart pair per multi-day job.
F4: taps and invoice issue only in the Swift app by design; the back office has no invoices.
F1: no task builds the back office web page.
F1: no task builds the web page or either app file store.
F1, F5: back office is an API with no page; the Swift package lacks a day view, Arrive and extension.
F1, F3, F4: no page; no Swift file store; refuses deleting a cleaner with future jobs.
F2, F4, F5, F7: a sketch with SwiftUI views; no CRUD, settlement or utilization; storage optional.
F1, F4, F5, F7: no page; storage left open; the Swift package only records taps and extensions.
F1, F2, F5, F7: almost everything in a Python API; the Swift package gets models and two tasks.
F1-F5, F7: a connected REST back end with a SwiftUI client.
F1-F5, F7: language, storage and platform left as NEEDS CLARIFICATION; neither app planned.
